summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.9% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the latest measurement period, up from 28.0% the prior period, making adoption both measurable and gradually rising across the sector. The range of applications spans the full property lifecycle: automated valuation at the data layer, leasing and tenant communication in day-to-day operations, document extraction in asset management, and portfolio analytics and building operations at the enterprise level.

Automated valuation models are the sector's oldest and most consequential AI deployment. Zillow publishes Zestimate valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network-based model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and historical data, and the company states that continuous refinement over nearly 20 years has helped reduce overall error rates. HouseCanary offers AI-powered valuations, forecasts, and analytics covering over 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning with image recognition that identifies room types and assesses home condition from photos. Opendoor deploys pricing models to make direct purchase offers to homeowners, a use case where model error carries direct balance-sheet consequences. On the commercial side, Prophia uses AI to extract key lease terms from documents and combines that extraction with expert validation to produce structured lease data, addressing one of the clearest document-AI problems in the sector.

The enterprise and operations layer is where the largest commercial players are concentrating investment. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, applying it across brokerage, facilities management, and portfolio analytics. Building Engines, a JLL company, offers an AI-powered property management platform called Prism that delivers recommendations and automation aimed at cutting costs and growing net operating income. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D data using cameras and computer vision, enabling virtual tours, floor plans, and integration with construction platforms such as Procore and Autodesk. EliseAI operates an agentic conversational AI platform for property management that handles leasing inquiries, schedules tours, follows up with prospects, and manages maintenance requests around the clock, with the stated aim of reducing overhead and freeing staff for higher-value work. Compass integrates AI into residential brokerage workflows covering agent tools and client-facing services.

The regulatory posture for this sector is more developed than most. The CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized a rule implementing quality control standards for automated valuation models under the Dodd-Frank Act. Institutions that use AVMs in credit decisions or securitization determinations must adopt policies and control systems ensuring high confidence in AVM estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and random sample testing and reviews. This makes AVM governance the first binding federal AI compliance obligation in real estate, and it falls on mortgage originators and secondary market issuers rather than the valuation platform vendors themselves.

The proptech investment and community infrastructure around these deployments is organized. CRETI, the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation, maintains a network of over 500 investors focused on built-world technology and runs a zero-equity accelerator for emerging proptech companies. CREtech convenes commercial real estate leaders around AI strategy, with its 2026 New York conference projecting 3,000 attendees and more than 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings. NAR REACH, created by Second Century Ventures, functions as the residential side's technology accelerator, vetting and scaling tools aimed at agents and brokerages. For a decision-maker evaluating deployment, the sector offers an unusually clear map: valuation AI is regulated and the compliance requirements are public, operations automation from leasing to building management has mature vendors with stated ROI claims, and the proptech capital network provides a structured way to evaluate emerging tools before committing at scale.
